extracted.intended_audience: literate London readers; aspiring writers, critics, and general readers interested in taste and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and moral reflection for writers, critics, and readers on literary criticism, style (especially metaphor), moral conduct (slander), dreaming and love-casuistics as presented in The Spectator essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a true Critick
rubrics_metrics.description: I have a great Esteem for a true Critick, such as Aristotle and Longinus among the Greeks, Horace and Quintilian among the Romans, Boileau and Dacier among the French. The Ancient Criticks are full of the Praises of their Contemporaries; they discover Beauties which escaped the Observation of the Vulgar, and very often find out Reasons for palliating and excusing such little Slips and Oversights as were committed in the Writings of eminent Authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be learned and tasteful (knowledge of ancient authors/languages); seek and praise beauties that common readers miss; temper judgment with charity toward eminent authors; explain small faults rather than deride. Examples: Aristotle, Horace, Boileau. Anti-pattern: unread, illiterate critics who judge only at second-hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failings of petty or envious critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the Smatterers in Criticism who appear among us, make it their Business to vilifie and depreciate every new Production that gains Applause, to descry imaginary Blemishes, and to prove by far-fetch'd Arguments, that what pass for Beauties in any celebrated Piece are Faults and Errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid criticizing successful works from envy or laziness. Do not invent far-fetched arguments to turn admired features into faults. Anti-pattern: critics who use unintelligible jargon (Unity, Action, Sentiment, Diction) to appear deep without real insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity is not a mark of badness (critic's fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several of them lay it down as a Maxim, That whatever Dramatick Performance has a long Run, must of Necessity be good for nothing; as though the first Precept in Poetry were not to please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a long run or popular success as evidence the work is worthless; the primary aim of poetry/drama is to please. Anti-pattern: dismissing popular works solely because they succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit deliberate deviation from rules when it yields higher beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is sometimes a greater Judgment shewn in deviating from the Rules of Art, than in adhering to them; and purposely receded from an established Rule of the Drama, when it has made way for a much higher Beauty than the Observation of such a Rule would have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that breaking established rules can be justified by superior artistic effect (the sublime, 'gusto grande'). Examples: ancient tragic writers and great masters of architecture/statuary who depart from art to greater effect. Anti-pattern: rigid adherence to rules at expense of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value genius and natural force over mere technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is more Beauty in the Works of a great Genius who is ignorant of all the Rules of Art, than in the Works of a little Genius, who not only knows, but scrupulously observes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the effect, vitality, and imaginative power of a work (e.g., Shakespeare) above flawless technical conformity. Example/appeal: Shakespeare preferred even with rule violations. Anti-pattern: preferring pedantic, 'correct' but lifeless writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper definition and use of Metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: A Metaphor is a Simile in one Word, which serves to convey the Thoughts of the Mind under Resemblances and Images which affect the Senses. Metaphors are Images of things which affect the Senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors as concise sensory images that illuminate thought. Ensure the metaphor is apt and comes from a coherent sensory domain. Consider whether the image genuinely conveys the intended idea. Anti-pattern: forced or irrelevant metaphors that obscure sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixture of inconsistent Metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mixture of inconsistent Metaphors, which is a Fault but too often found in learned Writers... an unskilful Author shall run these Metaphors so absurdly into one another, that there shall be no Simile, no agreeable Picture, no apt Resemblance, but Confusion, Obscurity, and Noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep metaphors homogeneous and consistent; do not combine images from incompatible domains (sight vs hearing, sea vs desert actions). Example of bad mixture: comparing a hero to a Thunderbolt, a Lion, and the Sea and then mixing their actions impossibly. Test: imagine the image painted—if it leads to absurdity, it's mixed. Anti-pattern: 'heavy Lashes that have dropped from your Pen'—mixed bodily/image incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let Metaphors run into tedious Allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: There is yet one Evil more... the running of Metaphors into tedious Allegories; which, though an Error on the better Hand, causes Confusion as much as the other... when the Lustre of one Word leads a Writer out of his Road, and makes him wander from his Subject for a Page together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep metaphors concise and subject-focused; avoid extended allegorical digressions that distract from the argument. Example anti-pattern: taking 'a world of charms' and treating the beloved as if possessing climate zones and poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination rules to detect a propensity for Slander
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall lay down three Rules by which I would have a Man examine and search into his own Heart... First of all, Let him consider whether he does not take Delight in hearing the Faults of others. Secondly, Whether he is not too apt to believe such little blackning Accounts, and more inclined to be credulous on the uncharitable than on the good-natured Side. Thirdly, Whether he is not ready to spread and propagate such Reports as tend to the Disreputation of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three checks as diagnostic criteria: (1) pleasure in others' faults, (2) credulity toward uncharitable reports, (3) readiness to propagate them. If any are true, one is culpable. Remedy: cultivate indifference to scandal and test reports by charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of charitable presumption on hearing bad accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fathers are there ordered, never to give an Ear to any Accounts of Base or Criminal Actions; to turn off all such Discourse if possible; but in Case they hear any thing of this Nature so well attested that they cannot disbelieve it, they are then to suppose, that the criminal Action may have proceeded from a good Intention in him who is guilty of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with allegations, avoid gossiping; if evidence is overwhelming, interpret the act with charitable motives where possible. Practice: refuse to entertain base accounts; change the subject; favor generous explanations of others' actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Dreams as potentially instructive and shaped by waking life
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy in Dreams gives us much such another Landskip of Life as that does of Countries... Our Dreams are generally conformable to our waking Thoughts, so that it is not impossible to convey our selves to a Consort of Musick, the Conversation of Distant Friends, or any other Entertainment which has been before lodged in the Mind. My Readers, by applying these Hints will find the Necessity of making a 'good Day' of it, if they heartily wish themselves a good Night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider dreams as meaningful traces worth examining; influence dreams by curating daytime impressions and activities. Practical tip: 'make a good Day' (fill waking hours with the things you wish to dream) and keep a noctuary to pursue insights. Anti-pattern: dismissing dreams as wholly valueless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize origins and uncontrollability of dream ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ideas which strike the Fancy, arise in us without our Choice, either from the Occurrences of the Day past, the Temper we lye down in, or it may be the Direction of some superior Being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that dreams often reflect recent experiences or mood; to influence dreams, manage daytime events and temper. Acknowledge limits: one does not fully command dreams, but can shape conditions. Use dreams as a source of creative material rather than literal forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love-casuist topics for judging courtship gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: He assures me... that he does not doubt of giving Judgment to the Satisfaction of the Parties concerned, on the most nice and intricate Cases which can happen in an Amour; as, How great the Contraction of the Fingers must be before it amounts to a Squeeze by the Hand. What can be properly termed an absolute Denial from a Maid, and what from a Widow. What Advances a Lover may presume to make, after having received a Patt upon his Shoulder from his Mistress's Fan. Whether a Lady, at the first Interview, may allow an Humble Servant to kiss her Hand. How far it may be permitted to caress the Maid in order to succeed with the Mistress. What Constructions a Man may put upon a Smile, and in what Cases a Frown goes for nothing. On what Occasions a sheepish Look may do Service, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a taxonomy of borderline courtship signals and the kinds of fine judgments ('casuistry') expected in resolving amorous ambiguities. Use as checklist topics when counseling lovers: interpret gestures, distinctions between denials, permissible advances, and reading smiles/frowns. Anti-pattern: crude literalism or ignoring social nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims in Love (practical aphorisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There are more Calamities in the World arising from Love than from Hatred. Love is the Daughter of Idleness, but the Mother of Disquietude. Men of grave Natures (says Sir Francis Bacon) are the most constant; for the same Reason Men should be more constant than Women. The Gay Part of Mankind is most amorous, the Serious most loving. A Coquet often loses her Reputation, whilst she preserves her Virtue. A Prude often preserves her Reputation when she has lost her Virtue. Love refines a Man's Behaviour, but makes a Woman's ridiculous. Love is generally accompanied with Good-will in the Young, Interest in the Middle-aged, and a Passion too gross to Name in the Old. The Endeavours to revive a decaying Passion generally extinguish the Remains of it. A Woman who from being a Slattern becomes over-neat, or from being over-neat becomes a Slattern, is most certainly in Love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concise rules/observations about the effects and social signs of love are presented as the result of long reflection and may be used as heuristics when reflecting on amorous behavior. Use them as aphoristic guides rather than strict laws; they offer ironic and observational counsel. Anti-pattern: treating aphorisms as universal scientific truths.
